The Ni-Co based superalloy has a service temperature of 750°C and exhibits excellent creep resistance, fatigue resistance, and structural stability.
The as-cast directionally solidified alloy has a columnar-grained microstructure with an average primary and secondary dendrite arm spacing of 363 ± 6 μm and 74 ± 2 μm, respectively.
The γ' precipitates in the interdendritic region are larger (800 nm) compared to the dendritic core (200 nm) due to segregation of alloying elements.
EPMA analysis shows that Ti is severely segregated in the eutectic (γ + γ') and η phases, while Al is more uniformly distributed.
The segregation coefficient k is greater than 1 for Co, Cr, and W, indicating reverse segregation, while it is less than 1 for Ti, indicating positive segregation.
The optimal single-stage homogenization process is determined to be 1180°C for 2 hours, which eliminates dendritic segregation without excessive grain growth.
The residual segregation index δ decreases from 1 to 0.29 for Ti and from 1 to 0.32 for W after homogenization at 1180°C for 4 hours.
The estimated diffusion coefficients of W and Ti at 1180°C are 11.02 × 10^-15 m^2/s and 11.97 × 10^-15 m^2/s, respectively.
The eutectic (γ + γ') and η phases gradually dissolve into the matrix with increasing homogenization temperature, and at 1180°C for 2 hours, only a few small particulate phases remain.
The homogenized microstructure with reduced segregation and precipitates is favorable for the subsequent hot deformation of the Ni-Co based superalloy.
Directional solidification is an effective method to produce Ni-Co based superalloys with a relatively uniform as-cast microstructure compared to traditional melting processes.
The high alloying degree of Ni-Co based superalloys renders them difficult to cast and wrought due to severe solidification segregation, low melting point, and inclusions.
Homogenization treatment is a critical step in the manufacturing process of cast and wrought superalloys to eliminate segregation and improve hot workability.
Residual segregation of elements during homogenization can have a seriously adverse impact on the subsequent hot-working process of refractory superalloys.
The homogenization process determines the success of the subsequent deformation as well as the performance of the turbine disk in aeroengines.
